sources.why: 8,000 BTU table, not the small unit or overnight
sources.evidence: An 8,000 BTU window unit uses about 533 W, so a 1,000 Wh station lasts under two hours with the compressor on.

sources.why: 5-6k BTU runtimes plus a named pick, framed for outages
sources.evidence: Yes, for a 5,000 to 6,000 BTU unit. It draws about 450 W averaged over an hour and surges to 1,500 W at startup

sources.why: overnight battery sizing for 5,000 BTU, but no station named
sources.evidence: For 8 hours of a 5,000 BTU unit, plan on about 2,100 Wh of battery (about 2,300 Wh with a 10% margin) and at least 1,200 W of surge.
A 1,000Wh battery runs an 8,000 BTU inverter AC drawing 530W for about 1.6 hours.

sources.why: home outage roundup, mostly larger units
sources.evidence: No station under $1,000 can reliably handle the surge draw of an 8,000 BTU or larger AC unit.
Smaller window ACs (around 5,000–8,000 BTU ) are the most realistic match.

sources.why: general van AC guide, no product pick
sources.evidence: Yes—a suitably sized portable power station can run an air conditioner. The harder question is whether it can start it safely and run it for long enough to be useful .

missing: A measured overnight (8-hour) runtime for a 5,000 BTU window AC on specific stations, with current prices, and a camping-focused pick that weighs portability, surge and solar recharge for a tent or camper.
why: No major reviewer or authority shows up. All the results are spec-math niche sites, listicles and one brand blog, mostly written for home outages. Only two name a pick for the 5,000 BTU case, and neither tested it. None gives a camping-specific, priced, overnight recommendation.
